=== PAGE 1 ===
Full-Stack Engineer Take-Home Problem:
Job Management Dashboard
Introduction
This take-home assignment is designed to evaluate your full-stack engineering skills, with a
particular emphasis on frontend development using React and TypeScript, and backend
development using Django and PostgreSQL. We're looking for clean, well-structured code, good
problem-solving abilities, and an understanding of how to build a deployable application.
The problem should be completable within approximately 4 hours. Please focus on delivering
a working solution that meets the core requirements. If you have time, feel free to tackle the
stretch goals.
Problem Statement: Simple Job Management Dashboard
the reviewer helps customers manage complex computational jobs. For this assignment, you will
build a simplified "Job Management Dashboard" where users can view, create, and manage the
status of computational jobs.
Core Requirements
1. Backend (Django & PostgreSQL)
○
Create a Django project with a single application.
○
Define a Job model with the following fields:
■
id: Primary key (automatically generated).
■
name: A string representing the job's name (e.g.,
"Fluid Dynamics
Simulation"
,
"ML Model Training").
■ created_at: Datetime field, automatically set on creation.
■ updated_at: Datetime field, automatically updated on each save.
○
Define a JobStatus model with the following fields:
■
id: Primary key (automatically generated).
■ job: A foreign key linking to the Job model.
■ status_type: A choice field with at least four distinct states (e.g.,
PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED).
■ timestamp: Datetime field, captures when the status was recorded.
○
Implement a RESTful API with the following endpoints:
=== PAGE 2 ===
■ GET /api/jobs/: List all jobs. This endpoint should include the
current status for each job (i.e., the status_type from the latest
JobStatus entry for that job).
■
POST /api/jobs/: Create a new job. Upon creation, an initial
JobStatus entry (e.g., PENDING) should be automatically created for
this job.
■
PATCH /api/jobs/<id>/: Update a job. This action should involve
creating a new JobStatus entry for the job with the updated
status_type.
■
DELETE /api/jobs/<id>/: Delete a specific job. Ensure that all
associated JobStatus entries are also deleted.
○
Configure the Django application to connect to a PostgreSQL database.
2. Frontend (React & TypeScript)
○
Create a React application (e.g., using Create React App or Vite).
○
Display a list of all jobs fetched from your Django backend. Each job in the list
should show its name and current status.
○
Provide a form or input field to allow users to create a new job by entering a
name.
○
For each job in the list, provide a mechanism (e.g., a dropdown, buttons, or a
modal) to update its status to any of the defined states. This action should trigger
the creation of a new JobStatus entry on the backend.
○
For each job, provide a button to delete it.
○
Implement basic error handling for API calls (e.g., display a simple message if
fetching or updating fails).
○
Implement simple client-side validation for the new job form (e.g., name cannot
be empty).
○
Ensure the UI updates dynamically after creating, updating, or deleting jobs.
Style the application using a method of your choice to make the UI presentable.
3. Testing
○
○
Include at least one End-to-End (E2E) test using Playwright. This test should
cover a critical user flow, such as:
■ Creating a new job and verifying it appears in the list with the correct
initial status.
■ Updating a job's status to a different available status and verifying the
change.
4. Deployment & Setup
○
Provide Dockerfiles for both your Django backend and your React frontend
(or a single Dockerfile for the backend and instructions for serving the React
build).
○
Provide a docker-compose.yml file that orchestrates your Django backend,
PostgreSQL database, and React frontend, allowing for easy setup and running
of the entire application with a single command.
=== PAGE 3 ===
○
Include a Makefile with the following commands:
■
make build: Builds the Docker images.
■
make up: Starts the entire application stack using Docker Compose.
■
make test: Runs your Playwright E2E tests.
■
make stop: Stops the running Docker containers.
■
make clean: Removes Docker volumes/networks if necessary for a
clean slate.
5. Performance Considerations
○
While building the application, consider web performance optimization. Imagine a
scenario where there could be millions of jobs in the database.
○
Address how you would efficiently fetch and display this large dataset in the
frontend.
○
Briefly describe any performance considerations you made or optimizations you
implemented in your README.md file
Stretch Goals (Optional)
If you complete the core requirements and have time remaining, consider implementing one or
more of the following:
●
Job Status History View: Allow users to view the full history of status changes for a
●
●
●
particular job.
Filtering/Sorting: Add functionality to filter jobs by current status or sort them by
name/creation date.
Job Details View: Allow users to click on a job to view more detailed information in a
separate page with a distinct URL from the job list page.
Frontend Unit Tests: Add unit tests for critical React components using React Testing
Library.
●
Backend Unit Tests: Add unit tests for your Django models or API views.
AI Usage Guidelines
We strongly encourage the use of AI-assisted developer tooling to implement this project. If
you do use AI, please include a screen recording or transcript link showing your interactions.
We are interested in evaluating AI fluency and not just the final output. While you are welcome

output, catch issues, and refine your approach.
Our expectation is that all engineers are able to walk through and explain the code as if it were
theirs. Be prepared to explain and extend your solution in a follow-up conversation.
Deliverables

●
●

docker-compose.yml file.

Correctness: Does the application meet all core requirements and function as

Before writing the plan, I need your input on four key decisions, since you'll have to defend them in the follow-up interview.

questions.question: How should the API get each job's current status when there are millions of jobs?

options.label: Denormalize (Recommended)
options.description: Add an indexed current_status column on Job, written in the same DB transaction as the JobStatus insert. JobStatus stays the append-only history. List is one indexed query, and the filter-by-status stretch goal becomes trivial later. Cost: one field beyond the spec's Job field list, which we justify in the README.

options.label: Subquery on read
options.description: Keep Job exactly as the spec lists it and annotate the latest JobStatus per row using a (job_id, timestamp DESC) index. Fine for listing one page, but filtering or sorting by status across millions of rows later would be slow.

questions.question: How should the job list page through a huge dataset? This drives both the API and the UI design.

options.label: Cursor + Prev/Next (Recommended)
options.description: Keyset (cursor) pagination in the API, AntD Table with Previous/Next and a page-size picker. Constant-time at any depth and no COUNT(*) over millions of rows. Trade-off: no 'jump to page 500' and no total count.

options.label: Cursor + infinite scroll
options.description: Same keyset API, but a virtualized list that loads more as you scroll. Feels modern, but is harder to make accessible and harder to test reliably in Playwright.

options.label: Numbered pages
options.description: Classic offset pagination with page numbers and a total. Most familiar UI, but OFFSET and COUNT(*) both degrade badly in Postgres at millions of rows.

questions.question: What should `make test` run, and how should we prove performance at scale? The evaluator stops if `make test` fails, so it must be fast and deterministic.

options.description: `make test` runs backend unit tests then Playwright. Unit tests include cheap perf guards (query-count assertions against N+1, EXPLAIN checks that the list uses the index). with no `total` it falls back to `dataSource.length` (client-side paging of what you handed it).

- A small `CursorPager` component under the table: two AntD `Button`s (Previous / Next) and a

```
CLAUDE.md                     # evaluation criteria + this plan + conventions
README.md

  Dockerfile  requirements.txt  manage.py  pytest.ini

    models.py  services.py  serializers.py  views.py  urls.py  pagination.py
    migrations/
    management/commands/seed_jobs.py
    tests/                    # test_models, test_api, test_services, test_perf
frontend/
  Dockerfile  nginx.conf  vite.config.ts  tsconfig.json

    api/client.ts  api/jobs.ts

e2e/
  Dockerfile  playwright.config.ts  tests/jobs.spec.ts
```

Each phase lists: goal, steps, exit check, and a short "learn" note mapped to your Flask/MySQL

- Write `CLAUDE.md` at the repo root containing: the evaluation criteria as a checklist
  (Correctness, Code Quality: readability / maintainability / modularity / error handling / type
  safety, Testing, Setup & Deployment, Problem Solving, Attention to Detail), the hard gate, scope,

features.
1. `backend/`: Django project `config`, app `jobs`, `GET /api/health/` that runs `SELECT 1`.
   Settings read DB config from env vars with working dev defaults (no `.env` needed on a clone).
2. `backend/Dockerfile`: pinned `python:3.x-slim`, copy `requirements.txt` and install before
   copying source, non-root user, gunicorn. Entrypoint runs `migrate` then starts the server.
3. `frontend/`: Vite React-TS app showing a title and the health result. `Dockerfile` is
   multi-stage: `node` builds, `nginx` serves `dist/` and proxies `/api/`.
4. `docker-compose.yml`: `db` (pinned `postgres`, named volume, `pg_isready` healthcheck),
   `backend` (healthcheck on `/api/health/`, `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy`),
   `frontend`, and `e2e` behind `profiles: [e2e]`.
5. `e2e/`: one Playwright smoke test: page loads and shows the backend as healthy.
6. `Makefile`: `build`, `up`, `test`, `stop`, `clean`, plus `logs`, `help`. `make test` brings up

   exit code, and always tears down with `down -v`.

  dir; `make up` shows the page in a browser.
- **Learn:**
  - Dockerfile layer caching: dependency files are copied before source so a code edit does not
    reinstall packages. Multi-stage builds keep node out of the final image.
  - `depends_on` only orders start-up; `condition: service_healthy` is what actually waits for
    Postgres. This is the most common cause of flaky compose stacks.
  - Makefile: recipes must be indented with tabs; `.PHONY` marks targets that are not files;
    `docker compose` (v2, a plugin) not `docker-compose` (v1).
  - `manage.py` is the `flask` CLI; `settings.py` is `app.config`; a Django "app" is roughly a
    Blueprint that also owns its models and migrations.

1. Tests first (`pytest-django`, real Postgres in the container, `make test-backend`):
   creation sets timestamps; `updated_at` moves on save; status choices are enforced; deleting a
   job removes its statuses; default `current_status` is `PENDING`.
2. `Job`: `name` (`CharField(max_length=255)`), `created_at` (`auto_now_add`), `updated_at`
   (`auto_now`), `current_status` (`TextChoices`, default `PENDING`).

   (`TextChoices`: PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED), `timestamp`; composite index
   `(job, -timestamp)` ready for the history stretch goal.
4. `# TODO` on `Job.Meta`: composite index `(current_status, -id)` deferred until filter-by-status
   is built (what: index for filtered listing; why deferred: no filter yet and every index taxes
   writes; fix: one `AddIndex` migration, built `CONCURRENTLY` in production).
- **Exit:** model tests green; migration file reviewed by you.
- **Learn:**
  - Django ORM is SQLAlchemy with the model and the table declared together; `makemigrations` +
    `migrate` is Alembic `revision --autogenerate` + `upgrade`.
  - Postgres vs MySQL: tables are heaps, not clustered on the PK like InnoDB, so "order by PK" is
    an index scan rather than free; DDL is transactional (a failed migration rolls back);
    `timestamptz` instead of `DATETIME`; identity columns instead of `AUTO_INCREMENT`.
  - Django's `CASCADE` is performed by the ORM (it collects and deletes children), not by a DB
    `ON DELETE CASCADE`. Fine per job; worth knowing for bulk deletes.

### Phase 3 — REST API (TDD)
1. Tests first, per endpoint, including failure paths:
   - `GET /api/jobs/`: returns `{next, previous, results}`; each result has `id`, `name`,
     `current_status`, `created_at`, `updated_at`; newest first; `page_size` capped.
   - `POST /api/jobs/`: 201; creates the job and exactly one `PENDING` status; blank /
     whitespace-only / over-long name gives 400 with a field error.
   - `PATCH /api/jobs/<id>/`: 200; appends a `JobStatus`; updates `current_status` and
     `updated_at`; invalid status gives 400; unknown id gives 404.
   - `DELETE /api/jobs/<id>/`: 204; statuses gone; second delete gives 404.
2. `services.py`: `create_job(name)` and `change_status(job_id, status)`, each in
   `transaction.atomic()`. `change_status` takes `select_for_update()` on the job row so two
   concurrent PATCHes cannot leave `current_status` disagreeing with the newest history row.
3. `serializers.py`, `views.py` (`ModelViewSet` limited to list/create/partial_update/destroy),
   `pagination.py` (`CursorPagination`, ordering `-id`, default 20, max 100), `urls.py` (router).

   failure handling, limits, concurrency, observability (request logging to stdout), tests.
- **Exit:** `make test-backend` green; `curl` walkthrough of all four endpoints via `make up`.
- **Learn:**
  - DRF serializer is marshmallow / pydantic: validation in, JSON out. A ViewSet + router is a
    `MethodView` registered on a Blueprint, with the URL table generated for you.
  - Thin views, logic in a service module: the same pattern as keeping Flask route functions thin.
  - `transaction.atomic()` is `with db.session.begin():`; `select_for_update()` is

1. `seed_jobs` management command: inserts N jobs + initial statuses with
   `INSERT ... SELECT generate_series(...)` (about 1M rows in seconds). `make seed N=1000000`.
2. Cheap guards inside the normal backend tests: list endpoint runs a constant number of queries
   regardless of page size (`django_assert_num_queries`), and `EXPLAIN` of the list query shows an
   index scan with no sequential scan.

   states: populated, empty, loading, load error, create validation error, delete confirmation.

   - Page title, then a one-line create form (name input + "Create job" button).
   - Table: Name | Status | Created | Actions. Status is a coloured `Tag` with text (never colour

   - Errors: inline `Alert` with Retry for load failures; toast `message` for mutation results.

  every control has an accessible name that includes the job name ("Change status for <name>").
  Comparable UIs: GitHub Actions run list, AWS Batch job list.

3. `features/jobs/hooks.ts`: `useJobs(cursor, pageSize)` and three mutations that invalidate the

4. Components per the approved design, each small and single-purpose. AntD `Form` rules for
   client-side validation (required, trimmed, max 255), mirroring the server rules.
5. Remove the Phase 1 health placeholder.
- **Exit:** manual walkthrough of create / update / delete / error states against `make up`;
  `tsc --noEmit` and lint clean inside the container build.

1. Replace the smoke test with real flows:
   - create a job, see it in the list with `PENDING`;
   - change its status, see the new status, and it survives a reload;
   - delete it, it disappears;
   - submit an empty name, see the validation message and no request sent.
2. Reliability rules: unique job name per test; role/label-based locators; web-first assertions,

- **Exit:** `make test` green 3 times in a row from a clean clone.

1. README: prerequisites, the Makefile commands, architecture sketch, API reference, performance

   would come next: status index, partitioning/archival, read replicas, virtualized rows), design
   decisions and trade-offs, deferred items, time spent, prompt-engineering writeup + transcript
   link.
2. Final audit against the CLAUDE.md criteria checklist.
3. Fresh-clone rehearsal on your Mac; if you have access to a Linux box or VM, there too.
- **Reminder:** the brief asks for a screen recording or transcript of the AI interaction. Export
  this session's transcript (and any later sessions) before submitting.

- **Status history:** `GET /api/jobs/<id>/statuses/` over the existing `(job, -timestamp)` index.
- **Filter / sort:** `?status=` on the list + the deferred `(current_status, -id)` index.
- **Details page:** add `react-router`; `features/jobs/JobDetailPage.tsx` reuses `StatusTag`.
- **Frontend unit tests:** components are already small and take data via props/hooks.

- `make stop` and `make clean` leave no containers, networks or volumes behind.

pages). A cursor API never counts, so: `<Table pagination={false} />` plus a small `CursorPager`

with no `total` it falls back to `dataSource.length` (client-side paging of what you handed it).

### Phase 3 — Services and REST API (TDD)
**3a. Services** (`services.py`): `create_job(name)`, `change_status(job_id, status)`, each in
`transaction.atomic()`. `change_status` locks the job row with `select_for_update()`, inserts the
`JobStatus`, then saves `current_status` and `updated_at`.

Sync tests (the two-table invariant: `job.current_status` equals the `status_type` of that job's
newest `JobStatus`, newest = highest `id`). One shared `assert_in_sync(job)` helper, used in:
- after `create_job`: exactly one status row, `PENDING`, in sync;
- after a sequence of changes: row count is 1 + N, in sync after each step;
- **rollback:** force the `Job` save to raise after the `JobStatus` insert; assert no new status
  row exists and `current_status` is unchanged (proves atomicity);
- **concurrency:** several threads call `change_status` on one job with different states
  (`django_db(transaction=True)`); assert row count is 1 + threads and in sync;
- **`updated_at` actually moves** after `change_status` (Django gotcha: `save(update_fields=[...])`
  skips `auto_now` fields unless they are listed);
- `change_status` on a missing or just-deleted job raises not-found, writes nothing;
- the API cannot write `current_status` directly: POST/PATCH bodies containing `current_status`
  do not change it;
- `seed_jobs` output is in sync (added in Phase 4).

**3b. API** (`serializers.py`, `views.py`, `pagination.py`, `urls.py`); viewset limited to
list / create / partial_update / destroy; no authentication classes (so no CSRF surprises).
- `GET /api/jobs/`: `{next, previous, results}`; fields `id`, `name`, `current_status`,
  `created_at`, `updated_at`; newest first; page of 20; walking `next` to the end returns every
  job exactly once; a garbage `cursor` gives a 4xx, not a 500; empty table gives empty results.
- `POST /api/jobs/`: 201 + one `PENDING` row; blank, whitespace-only, missing, over-255 and
  NUL-containing names give 400 with a field error; surrounding whitespace is trimmed; duplicate
  names are allowed.
- `PATCH /api/jobs/<id>/`: 200 + appended row; missing / unknown / wrong-case `status_type` gives
  400 and writes nothing; unknown id gives 404; same status as current still appends.
- `DELETE /api/jobs/<id>/`: 204 with empty body; statuses gone; second delete gives 404.
- Any id that is non-numeric or larger than a bigint gives 404, not 500.
- PUT and `GET /api/jobs/<id>/` give 405 (not in the brief).

- **Two-table sync:** Phase 3 has a dedicated set of sync tests around one invariant: `current_status` equals the newest `JobStatus` row. They cover create, a sequence of changes, a forced mid-transaction failure (rollback), concurrent updates from several threads, and the API being unable to write `current_status` directly.
- **History index:** you were right; it is now a `TODO`. Only the history stretch goal would use it.
- **`make perf`:** it was over-design, so it's cut. The brief asks you to consider and describe performance, not benchmark it. What remains is a small seed command and two tests (no N+1; the list query uses the index), marked first to cut.
- **Scope:** I checked every core bullet in the brief against a phase. Also cut: the page-size selector, the validation E2E test, `make logs`, and the "Created" column (a design-step question now).

The critique turned up these likely bugs, each now with a test or a handling rule in the plan:

- **Status choices not enforced:** Django `choices` are not checked on `save()`, so a bad status could be stored. Fix: database check constraints.
- **`updated_at` not moving:** a partial save skips auto-updated fields unless they are listed.
- **Host header in the test stack:** the browser calls `http://frontend`, which Django rejects with 400 unless `ALLOWED_HOSTS` allows it. This would have broken the gate.
- **Index test on a tiny table:** Postgres picks a full scan when the table is small, so the test seeds about 20k rows first.
- **Bad ids and cursors:** a non-numeric or oversized id, or a garbage cursor, must give a 4xx rather than a 500.
- **Frontend client:** DELETE returns no body, and nginx returns non-JSON when the backend is down; both crash a naive `response.json()`.
- **Paging edge cases:** deleting the last row on a page, or a stale cursor, resets to the first page.
- **Double-create:** the submit button is disabled while the request is in flight.

On `EXPLAIN`, since you asked for more:

- **What it does:** `EXPLAIN <query>` prints the plan Postgres would use without running it. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs the query and adds real timings and row counts, so wrap writes in a transaction you roll back.
- **How to read it:** it is a tree, read from the innermost line outward. Each line is a step, with an estimated cost and row count.
- **MySQL equivalents:** `Seq Scan` is `type: ALL` (full table scan), `Index Scan` is `ref`/`range`, `Index Only Scan` is "Using index", and a `Sort` step is "Using filesort".
- **What we want for the job list:** a `Limit` over an `Index Scan Backward` on the primary key, touching about 21 rows. An offset query has the same shape but shows the scan reading and discarding every skipped row, which is why deep pages get slow.
- **Estimates vs actuals:** if estimated and actual row counts differ wildly, the table statistics are stale; `ANALYZE <table>` refreshes them.
- **From Django:** `queryset.explain(analyze=True)` returns the same output.

message.content: i normally use pytest, is pytest-django anything special? and why are we using it over pytest

content.text:
`pytest-django` isn't a replacement for pytest; it's a pytest plugin, so you're still writing plain pytest tests (functions, fixtures, `assert`, parametrize). It's the equivalent of `pytest-flask` in your current stack.

Plain pytest alone doesn't work well with Django, because Django needs setup before any model can be imported. The plugin does three things you'd otherwise hand-write in `conftest.py`:

- **Boots Django:** it reads `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE` from `pytest.ini` and calls `django.setup()` before collection. Without it, importing `jobs.models` fails with "apps aren't loaded yet".
- **Manages the test database:** it creates a separate `test_<dbname>` database, runs migrations once per session, and wraps each test in a transaction that is rolled back, so tests don't leak rows into each other. In Flask you'd have written this yourself as a session-scoped fixture with `create_all()` and a rollback per test.
- **Provides fixtures:** `client` (like Flask's `app.test_client()`), `django_assert_num_queries` (which the no-N+1 test in Phase 4 uses), and `settings` for per-test overrides.

Database access is opt-in per test via `@pytest.mark.django_db`, and a test that touches the DB without the mark fails loudly. The concurrency test in Phase 3 needs `@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)`: the default rollback-per-test wrapper keeps everything in one uncommitted transaction, so other threads would never see the rows. That mode really commits and then truncates the tables afterwards, which is slower, so we use it for that one test only.

The real alternative isn't plain pytest but Django's built-in runner (`manage.py test`, `unittest`-style `TestCase` classes). That works fine and saves one dependency. I picked `pytest-django` because you already know pytest, so you only have to learn the Django parts, and because DRF's own test client (`APIClient`) works with it unchanged.
